scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The imported Roman Republic from c.400 to c.1 BCE is coverage, not the historically conventional c.509–27 BCE lifespan. Early dates come from much later literary sources; Oakley’s chapter abstract explicitly cautions against precise early constitutional reconstruction. Roman Empire map feature exists but no checked target geometry at the 27 BCE event year, so no successor link is asserted.

Met essay main text establishes wealthy plebeian political equality in 287 BCE, not universal citizenship or equality; expansion mixed conquest and diplomacy and involved unequal gains. Caesar’s assassination in 44 BCE is distinct from the Augustan settlement in 27 BCE. No claim that a single act ended every republican practice.

UNESCO Via Appia main brief synthesis covers initial Rome–Capua road from 312 BCE, later extension and toll-free travel; the whole present 800 km and later amenities are not assigned to 312 BCE. Met villa wall painting date c.50–40 BCE differs from 79 CE burial; one elite room does not typify all homes. Tivoli group has qualified findspot, named owner inscriptions and hypothesised burial motive; no secure excavated provenance or cause of concealment claimed.

Cato On Agriculture 84–85 is one surviving landowner text, not evidence that every Roman ate these foods or that Punic porridge verifies Carthaginian cooking. Rowland/Howe Cambridge excerpt page 8 covers late Republic and early Empire education generally; the short account here limits itself to late-Republic patterns and unequal access. Enslaved pedagogue is not treated as free staff.

British Museum votive dated third to first centuries BCE only supports dedicating a breast model at a healing shrine, not diagnosis, person, efficacy or universal medicine. Ammerman Antiquity article documents the Forum drain and flood exposure, not household toilet or sewer connection rates. Roman latrine anecdotes from Imperial Ostia are excluded from this Republican card.

Met coin catalogue gives a 46 BCE Rome-minted gold coin and original inscription C·CAESAR COS·TER. Latin is the language, Roman alphabet the script. COS TER is abbreviated “consul for the third time”; Gaius resolves conventional C. abbreviation. Coin does not imply widespread literacy or gold-coin ownership. Original script specimen is from a dated object, not a later literary copy.

All imported geometry and historical basemap records unchanged. New text remains pending independent review. Mechanical audits, local phone/desktop inspection and public-page verification are publication checks, not an independent historical certification.

proposedOverrides.summary: The Roman Republic grew from a city-state into a Mediterranean power. The map shows selected centuries of that history; Caesar’s assassination in 44 BCE and the Augustan settlement in 27 BCE mark different steps in its political ending.
